summary: DHCP gives IPv4 hosts addressing and configuration information. This informational RFC discusses the identifiers DHCP carries and the privacy problems they may cause, such as letting observers recognize and track a device.

plainLanguage.summary: When a device asks for an address over DHCP, the request carries several values that stay the same over time. This document lists those values, explains what each one reveals, and shows how an observer on the network can use them to recognise a device, follow it around and work out what it is.

subtitle: What a DHCP request tells an observer about the device that sent it, and how the protocol leaks that information.

tldr.problem: DHCP gives IPv4 hosts their address and configuration, and the messages it uses carry several identifiers that can reveal a device's type, its operating system, where it is and where it has been.
tldr.mechanism: The document goes through the options that carry identifiers, such as the Client Identifier, the client FQDN and the relay agent information, and through the ways a server allocates addresses, then lists the attacks that use them.
tldr.outcome: It is an analysis, not a fix: the document says that protocol changes to address the problems are out of scope, and it points out that client privacy and client authentication are in practice mutually exclusive.

today: RFC 7819 is an Informational document published in April 2016. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it states that protocol changes to fix the privacy problems it analyses are out of scope for the document itself.

sections.title: Why DHCP Leaks Information
sections.content:
The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP), described in RFC 2131, provides addressing and configuration information to IPv4 hosts. DHCP uses several identifiers, and these can become a source of information about the IPv4 host. That information may include the device type, operating system information, and locations that the device may have previously visited.

The document defines a stable identifier as any property disclosed by a DHCP client that does not change over time, or changes very infrequently, and that is unique for that client in a given context. Examples given are the MAC address, the client identifier and a hostname. Some identifiers may be stable only under certain conditions: one client implementation may keep its client identifier in stable storage, while another may generate it on the fly and use a different one after each boot. Stable identifiers may or may not be globally unique.

The focus is on privacy for clients, to support client mobility and connection to random networks. The privacy of DHCP servers and relay agents is considered less important, because they are typically open for public services, and communication from a relay agent to a server is generally assumed to be protected from casual snooping because it travels in the provider's backbone. The document still explores those topics to some degree. It does not propose protocol changes to fix the problems it analyses; that work is explicitly out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Some values a device sends during DHCP never change. Once an observer has seen one of them, the observer can recognise the same device later, even on a different network. This document is a catalogue of those values and of what they give away.

sections.title: DHCP Options That Carry Identifiers
sections.content:
The Client Identifier option passes an explicit client identifier to a DHCP server. The identifier is an opaque key that must be unique to that client within the subnet it is attached to, and it typically stays stable after it has first been generated. It may hold a hardware address identical to the contents of the chaddr field, or another kind of identifier such as a DNS name. Clients are expected to generate their client identifiers once, during first operation, and store them in non-volatile storage, or to use a deterministic algorithm that produces the same values again.

In practice an implementation uses the available link-layer address during its first boot. Even if the administrator later enables link-layer address randomization, it was probably not enabled during that first boot, so the original, unobfuscated link-layer address is likely to end up being announced as the client identifier. Exposing the original link-layer address there also undermines other privacy extensions, such as RFC 4941.

The DHCP message header has htype and chaddr fields for the client link-layer address type and the link-layer address itself, and chaddr is used both as the hardware address for sending replies and as a client identifier. The yiaddr field conveys an allocated address from the server to the client, and the requested IP address option lets a client suggest a particular address.

The Client FQDN option lets clients and servers exchange information about the client's fully qualified domain name and about who updates the DNS with the associated A and PTR records. The Vendor Class, Vendor-Identifying Vendor Class and Vendor-Identifying Vendor Information options are used by the client to identify the vendor that manufactured the hardware, and their data area may hold further detail such as the version of the operating system or the amount of memory installed.

Servers use the Civic Location option to deliver location information to clients, referring to the location of the server, of the network element believed to be closest to the client, or of the client itself. The GeoConf and GeoLoc options provide coordinate-based location. The Client System Architecture Type option lists supported architecture types, for clients booted over the network rather than from local storage.

Relay agents add a Relay Agent Information option with a circuit ID suboption, an agent-local identifier of the circuit a client-to-server packet arrived on, and a remote ID suboption holding a trusted identifier for the remote high-speed modem. The link-selection suboption names a subnet or link that can identify the client's subnet and, if the network topology is known, reveals the client's location. Relay agents also add a Subscriber-ID option, an ASCII string assigned by the network provider that is meant to stay the same as customers connect through different paths.
sections.plainLanguage: DHCP clients send several optional values, and most of them are designed to help the server recognise the same device again. That is exactly what makes them useful for tracking. The values include a client identifier, a hostname, a vendor name, and identifiers added by the relay agent that describes the physical line the device is on.

sections.title: How Address Allocation Affects Privacy
sections.content:
A DHCP server in the typical stateful mode manages one or more pools of IP addresses and picks an address out of a configured pool when a client asks. Depending on the implementation, several allocation strategies are possible, and the choice has privacy implications. The constraints in DHCP and DHCPv6 are radically different, but servers that allow the strategy to be configured may allow it in both.

Iterative allocation hands out addresses one by one. It is very fast, which is why deployments that prefer performance favour it, but it makes the allocated addresses very predictable. Because the addresses tend to cluster at the beginning of the available pool, it also makes scanning attacks much easier.

Identifier-based allocation picks an address based on one of the available identifiers, such as the client identifier or MAC address. It is convenient, since a returning client is very likely to get the same address, and system administrators often ask for it. The downside is a very stable IP address for the client, which means correlation of activities over time, location tracking, address scanning and vendor or operating system discovery all apply. Because the IPv4 address space is much smaller, this is almost never a problem in DHCP, but it certainly is in DHCPv6.

Hash allocation is an extension of identifier-based allocation that hashes the identifier first. If the hash is implemented correctly it removes the flaw of disclosing the identifier, which eliminates susceptibility to address scanning and to vendor or operating system discovery. If the hash is poorly implemented, for example if it can be reversed, it introduces no improvement over identifier-based allocation.

Random allocation picks a resource at random from the available pool, which essentially prevents a returning client from getting the same address again. It is beneficial from a privacy point of view, because such addresses are not susceptible to correlation attacks or to vendor, operating system or identity discovery attacks. Even so, a client may still be exposed if other information is disclosed elsewhere, for example when the address is randomized but the MAC address still leaks in the Client Identifier option. Given the limited size of most IPv4 public address pools, allocation mechanisms in IPv4 may not provide much privacy protection or leak much useful information, if misused.
sections.plainLanguage: The way a server hands out addresses changes how much it reveals. Handing out addresses in order makes them predictable. Deriving an address from the device's own identifier gives the device an address that never changes. Hashing the identifier breaks the link, as long as the hash cannot be reversed. Choosing an address at random breaks it too, but only if nothing else in the exchange gives the device away.

sections.title: What an Attacker Can Learn
sections.content:
The document lists what an attacker can derive from DHCP messages. The type of device can be guessed from the Vendor Class option, the chaddr field and by parsing the Client ID option, all of which may contain an Organizationally Unique Identifier representing the device's vendor, and that knowledge can be used for device-specific vulnerability exploitation attacks. The operating system can be guessed from the Vendor Class option, the Client System Architecture Type option, or by fingerprinting the combination of options the client asks for in the Parameter Request List.

Location information comes most directly from a server message carrying the Civic Location, GeoConf or GeoLoc options, and can also be inferred from the Relay Agent Information option with its remote ID or circuit ID suboptions, or from the Subscriber ID option where the attacker has access to subscriber information.

When a client connects to a network it tries to get the address it had before, by putting the previously assigned address in the requested IP address option, and by observing those addresses an attacker can identify the network the client visited previously. A stable identity taken from the Client FQDN option, the Subscriber ID option or the Client ID option lets an attacker correlate the activities of a client across unrelated networks, and the FQDN can also be correlated with web server activity logs.

Pervasive monitoring is widespread and often covert surveillance through intrusive gathering of protocol artifacts, including application content or protocol metadata such as headers. An operator who controls a nontrivial number of access points or network segments may use what they learn about a single client to observe that client's habits. Users may not expect true privacy from their operators, but information set up to be monitored by a user's service operator may also be gathered by an adversary who monitors a wide range of networks.

Many deployments use DNS updates to put the client's current address and hostname into the DNS, where anyone can look them up. The client ID is also disclosed there, in the form of a SHA-256 digest, which cannot be converted back into the client ID but is still usable as a unique identifier accessible to any host. An IP address can correlate a host's activities for at least as long as the lifetime of the address, and if that address was generated from a stable identifier by a scheme the attacker can deduce, the correlation lasts as long as the identifier, often the lifetime of the device itself.

For location tracking, both passive and active methods work. A service the client connects to can log the client's address and draw conclusions about its location and movement. An attacker can also send ICMP echo requests or other probe packets to networks where the client is suspected to be. Attackers may also pretend to be an access concentrator, as a DHCP relay agent or as a DHCP client, to obtain location information directly from the server using the leasequery mechanism, or use bulk leasequery to obtain bulk information about DHCP bindings even without knowing the target bindings. Active leasequery subscribes to DHCP lease update changes in near real time; if it is misused, an attacker could defeat the server's authentication mechanisms and keep receiving updates without any local presence.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything the client sends can be turned against it. The vendor and hardware details point to known weaknesses. The address a client asks for reveals where it was last time. A hostname or a hashed client identifier lets one observer recognise the same device across many networks, and that is enough to follow a person's movements.

sections.title: Privacy and Authentication Pull Against Each Other
sections.content:
The security considerations section makes a single point about a trade-off that sits underneath all of the above. In current practice, client privacy and client authentication are mutually exclusive, because the client authentication procedure reveals additional client information in the certificates and identifiers it uses. Full privacy for clients may mean the clients are also anonymous to the server and to the network.

The privacy considerations section adds nothing further: the document as a whole discusses privacy in DHCP, so it says no dedicated discussion is needed. The document's own framing is that it analyses the identifiers DHCP uses and the problems they cause, and leaves the fixing to future work.
sections.plainLanguage: Authenticating a client means showing who it is, and that is the opposite of hiding. In current practice a network that authenticates its clients gives up some of the privacy that an anonymous client would have had.

viz.caption: FOUR WAYS A SERVER CAN PICK AN ADDRESS (RFC 7819, SECTION 4.2)

items.title: Iterative
items.text: Addresses are handed out one by one. Fast, but predictable, and clustered at the start of the pool.

items.title: Identifier-based
items.text: The address comes from the client identifier or MAC address. Convenient, but the address never changes.

items.title: Hash
items.text: The identifier is hashed first. This removes the link, but only if the hash cannot be reversed.

items.title: Random
items.text: The address is picked at random from the pool. Hard to correlate, but only if nothing else gives the client away.

viz.caption: WHAT CAN BE LEARNED FROM DHCP TRAFFIC (RFC 7819, SECTION 5)

items.title: Device type
items.text: Guessed from the Vendor Class option, the chaddr field and the Client ID option.

items.title: Operating system
items.text: Guessed from the Vendor Class option, the architecture type option, or the set of options requested.

items.title: Location
items.text: Read from the Civic Location and coordinate options, or inferred from relay agent information.

items.title: Previously visited networks
items.text: Seen in the requested IP address option, which carries the address used on a previous network.

items.title: A stable identity
items.text: The Client FQDN, Subscriber ID and Client ID options can all serve as long-lived identifiers.

items.title: Current address and hostname
items.text: Published in the DNS by DHCP updates, where anyone can look them up.

items.title: Correlation over time
items.text: An address identifies a host for as long as it lives, and longer if it was derived from a stable identifier.

items.title: Lease records
items.text: Leasequery and bulk leasequery can be misused to obtain bindings and location information.
